chapters.title: Chapter 5: Beyond Equality: KKT Conditions and Inequality Constraints

lessons.title: Complementary Slackness: When a Constraint "Binds" and When It Doesn't

children.text: The two-asset hedge example had an easy shortcut: only one constraint could possibly bind, so guessing which one was trivial. The interviewer's next problem has three assets, and Ananya has no way of knowing in advance which, if any, of the three no-short-selling rules actually bind. This lesson builds the systematic procedure for finding out, instead of guessing and hoping.

body.text: Since you cannot know in advance which constraints bind, test hypotheses systematically. Start with the cheapest guess, nothing binds, and if that fails, the specific way it failed tells you exactly what to guess next. Checking every KKT condition on each candidate tells you immediately whether the guess was right.

children.text: The Active-Set Method: Guess, Solve, Verify

Three repeatable steps: guess which constraints bind, solve the resulting equality-only problem (exactly Chapter 4's machinery, since a hypothesized-binding inequality just becomes a fixed equality for that guess), then verify every KKT condition against the result. If everything checks out, Chapter 2's convexity guarantee means this candidate is the true global optimum, not just a plausible one. If something fails, the failure itself points to the next guess.

Always start here, it is the cheapest check: solve the ordinary equality-only minimum variance problem and see if it happens to already satisfy every inequality constraint. Three assets: a volatile small-cap stock (40% volatility), a calmer large-cap stock (20% volatility, correlated 0.9 with the small-cap), and a gold ETF (15% volatility, weakly correlated with both at 0.05).

body.text: Step 1's guess fails: -30.4% violates the small-cap stock's no-short-selling constraint outright. But the failure is informative, not a dead end. It tells you exactly which constraint to hypothesize as binding next.

children.text: Step 2: Use the Violation to Guess Again

Hypothesize that only the small-cap stock's constraint binds: fix its weight at exactly 0, and re-solve for the remaining two assets as their own, smaller, two-asset minimum variance problem, using the exact closed-form formula from Chapter 3.

body.caption: The reduced two-asset sub-problem, ignoring the small-cap stock entirely.
The new candidate: excluded small-cap, the rest split between large-cap and gold.
Computed at the candidate w = (0, 0.3529, 0.6471). The last two entries match, as expected for the free assets.
Solve nu from either free asset (both agree), then lambda1 from the fixed asset's stationarity equation.

body.text: All four conditions check out, so this candidate is confirmed as the true, globally optimal, long-only minimum variance portfolio. Notice what would have happened with a wrong guess: hypothesizing instead that gold's constraint binds (fixing gold at 0, solving small-cap and large-cap alone) reproduces the exact -57% weight from the original two-asset hedge example, still negative, still infeasible. That wrong hypothesis is caught immediately, the reduced solve itself hands back an infeasible number for what was supposed to be a free variable. The method is self-correcting: a wrong guess never silently produces a plausible-looking wrong answer, it fails a check.

body.title: Read a failed verification
body.question: You hypothesize that a particular stock's no-short-selling constraint binds, fix its weight at 0, solve the reduced problem for the remaining stocks, and then compute that stock's implied multiplier as -0.02. What does this tell you?
options: The hypothesis is confirmed, since a multiplier was successfully computed
The hypothesis is wrong: dual feasibility requires the multiplier to be non-negative, so a negative value means this stock's constraint does not actually bind here
The covariance matrix must be invalid
Nothing; multiplier sign does not matter for verification
body.explanation: Dual feasibility requires every inequality multiplier to be non-negative. A negative computed multiplier means the hypothesis, that this particular constraint binds, is inconsistent with the KKT conditions. The correct next step is to guess a different subset of binding constraints and re-verify.

body.title: Plan the search for a four-asset portfolio
body.scenario: You are solving a long-only minimum variance problem with four stocks. Your first guess, nothing binds, produces two negative weights, on Stock B and Stock D.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's method, what should your next hypothesis be, and what would you need to check to confirm it?
body.modelAnswer: The natural next hypothesis is that both violated constraints bind at once: fix Stock B and Stock D at weight 0, and re-solve the reduced problem for Stock A and Stock C alone as their own two-asset minimum variance sub-problem. Once solved, check all four KKT conditions on the four-stock candidate: primal feasibility (all weights ≥ 0, budget satisfied), and dual feasibility, computing the implied multipliers for B and D from their stationarity equations and confirming both come out non-negative. If either multiplier is negative, that specific hypothesis is wrong and a different combination needs to be tried next.

body.title: Complementary Slackness in Practice: Core Terms

cards.definition: Guess which constraints bind, solve the resulting equality-only problem, then verify every KKT condition. Repeat with a new guess if verification fails.
An assumption about which specific inequality constraints hold exactly at their boundary, tested by solving the reduced problem and checking dual feasibility.
The smaller equality-only problem left after fixing every hypothesized-binding variable, solved using exactly Chapter 3 and 4's methods.

A wrong binding hypothesis never produces a plausible wrong answer; it fails either primal feasibility (a fixed variable's reduced solve implies infeasibility elsewhere) or dual feasibility (a negative multiplier).

points: Since you cannot know in advance which inequality constraints bind, test hypotheses systematically: guess, solve the resulting equality-only problem, and verify every KKT condition.
Always start by assuming nothing binds, the cheapest check. If it fails, the specific violated constraints tell you exactly what to hypothesize next.

For the three-asset small-cap, large-cap, gold example, the unconstrained solution wants to short the small-cap stock by about 30%; fixing that stock at zero and re-solving for the other two gives a candidate that passes every KKT check.
A wrong binding hypothesis is caught immediately, either by an infeasible reduced solve or by a negative implied multiplier, never by silently producing a plausible-looking wrong answer.
Because the underlying problem is convex (Chapter 2), a candidate that passes all four KKT conditions is guaranteed to be the true global optimum, not just a locally good guess.
The next lesson scales this exact procedure up to a full long-only minimum variance case study with more assets.
